channel.title: The Brand Identity – Features
channel.description: Graphic and brand design projects, interviews, and insights.

item.title: From Manchester to Apple: how Neil Nisbet learned what simple means
item.description: Neil Nisbet is a designer, creative director and musician whose work has moved between art, architecture, technology and culture for more than two decades. Through Buro Blank, his independent design practice, he works with companies in frontier technology, professional services and the built environment on identity, digital experiences and the visual expression of value. Alongside it, he maintains a music and audiovisual practice under the name Neil Blank, which acts as a creative catalyst for his commercial work. Raised outside Manchester, and now based in Los Angeles, Nisbet has built an unusually wide field of reference, from 2000 AD and Francis Bacon to Factory Records, Massimo Vignelli and Apple. We spoke about why minimalism can be sexy, how far a brand should misbehave, and why knowing where visual language has been is useful when you’re trying to work out where it might go next.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Studio Bright Green’s quietly confident identity for Levrant
item.description: London-based Studio Bright Green has created the identity for Levrant, a UK practice that works on historic buildings across architecture, heritage consultancy and townscape. Research with the practice’s team and its clients led to a name change and a visual language built around quiet confidence. That confidence runs through everything, from the typography and colour to the photography and the materials the team works with every day.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Ashfall Studio extends Carnilove’s pet food identity into a system
item.description: Carnilove is a premium pet-food brand that is sold in more than 80 markets, with an identity that Design Bridge and Partners created around the tension between the domestic pet and its wilder instincts. Prague-based design and technology partner Ashfall Studio came on board to take that identity further, spending 18 months developing it into a system for Carnilove’s teams to use across all of those markets.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: How New Apology branded ET AL for creators without factory contact
item.description: ET AL produces apparel for creative people, young clothing brands and small teams, taking on sourcing, sampling, production and delivery, as well as inventory and reorders after launch. Its customers have had to choose between print-on-demand, which is easy but generic, and traditional production, with its high minimums and months spent chasing factories. Provo-based design studio New Apology was brought in to create ET AL’s brand strategy, identity and website, as well as to art-direct all of its photography. “Together, we rallied around the concept of ‘pre-commerce’ and the thesis that ‘taste deserves infrastructure,’” explains New Apology’s founder Lyman Ballif. “Fashion and apparel production are notoriously gatekept industries where access usually requires decades of supply-chain networking. If ET AL is democratising that access, the brand needs to feel just as approachable to a creator in Des Moines, Iowa, as it does to an insider in New York.”
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Why do brand guidelines written for people fall short for AI agents?
item.description: What happens to a brand once AI agents start producing work alongside people, and where does it go wrong? Frontify, the brand intelligence tool for guidelines, assets and knowledge, has dozens of conversations every week with companies about the problems they are facing. “Everybody’s kind of going through roughly the same thing, but they just don’t speak to each other,” Senior Creative Director Hugo Timm, a Brazilian-British designer who has led Frontify’s in-house studio since 2024, tells us. “Teams really want help with automation,” he explains. “A lot of times, they’re facing pressure from above to become more efficient, or to distribute the tools to other teams, and they’re not entirely sure how to find their way towards agentic production.”
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Twice Shy positions Tula Louise as a soap atelier through a rebrand
item.description: Tula Louise is a soap brand that Jowanda Daley-Thomas started during COVID, when she began experimenting with natural pigments. Independent branding studio Twice Shy was commissioned to rework the brand as it stood, from strategy and positioning to the identity, logo, art direction and packaging design.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: A sub-45-minute 10K gave Tinloof the concept for Enroute’s identity
item.description: Enroute is a running/cycling store and community based in Vancouver that had gone for years without a clearly defined identity. With plans to grow beyond Canada, new retail stores and its first mobile app ahead, Enroute commissioned design and development agency Tinloof to create its first proper brand strategy, visual and motion identity, online store and app design. Tinloof added a watch app, too. “We needed a clear identity to root ourselves in,” explains Enroute’s founder, Sebastian Salas, a former professional athlete. “This would allow us to move confidently and create one Enroute experience across physical and online stores.”
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Jan Eumann on why Koto Berlin won’t stamp “a Koto look onto everything”
item.description: Koto is moving its Berlin operation into a studio with a lot more space – enough to double the size of its team. Executive Creative Director Jan Eumann joined from Wolff Olins as part of that expansion, arriving back in Germany after more than 12 years working in branding in the US. The studio now has 20 people from nine nationalities, many of whom moved to Berlin to work there. Eumann sees “a huge opportunity in Germany and the wider German-speaking market” and a chance to help US companies “find their feet in Europe.” In this interview, he talks to us about the studio’s push further into digital and campaigns, why it is “not interested in stamping a Koto look onto everything” and why “bigger only matters if the work gets better, too.”
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Survive the fiscal year in Better Half / Cult Holdings’ game for Brex
item.description: Fiscal Mania is an original arcade game in which players have to survive a fiscal year. New York-based creative studio Better Half / Cult Holdings created it for Brex, a finance platform for growing companies, along with the arcade cabinets that house it, a microsite and launch events in New York and San Francisco.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: How Afternow put Kinetik’s identity and four products into one system
item.description: Kinetik is a healthcare transportation platform that gets members to their appointments, working with health plans, brokers and transportation providers. Croatian agency Afternow has worked with Kinetik for four years, leading its rebrand, redesigning its website twice and rebuilding the design system behind four of its products.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Children’s curiosity leads Kind Studio’s Hatching Dragons rebrand
item.description: Hatching Dragons is a group of multilingual nurseries in London whose brand had fallen behind what the business had become. “When we started, Hatching Dragons was known as a bilingual Mandarin nursery,” explains Head of Brand & Marketing Marisa Forstyk. “That was true, but it was no longer the whole story. Our curriculum had evolved, and we’d come to see ourselves as early-years development specialists.”
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Superior Type’s Heaven is a sans serif built on oversized round shapes
item.description: Superior Type’s Heaven is a brutalist grotesque built on round shapes that are too big for their space. Drawn by type designer Petr Kucera, it comes as four families – Heaven 01, 03, 06 and 09 – each with 18 styles from Thin to Black, including italics, in Latin and Cyrillic. A SuperVariable version lets you set the weight to any point between the soft 01 and the boxy 09.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: How OB Studio took Reci from a prototype to an identity and live app
item.description: Reci is a private, invite-only app where people save, share and request service recommendations within a trusted circle of friends. When the Reci team reached out to Paris and London-based OB Studio, the app existed as its first web prototype, built to test that idea. “The next step was a mobile app that could be put in front of real users, and a brand that appealed to the people it was built for,” explains OB Studio’s Co-founder Julie Daled. The studio created the identity, then designed the mobile app and spent four weeks developing it. “Running all three phases with one team kept the decisions connected, from the first brand route to the live product,” she adds.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Studio Kiln designs an identity for Reset that adapts like its app
item.description: Reset is a weight-loss app for people who would rather not count every calorie. A 30-second face scan, read alongside a person’s answers about their habits and where they have struggled to lose weight, places them in one of five Reset types. Ester, Reset’s guide inside the app, then asks questions, learns from the answers and builds a person’s meals around that type – taking the effort out of deciding what and when to eat.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: The new rules of finance branding, explained by Koto’s Tom Moloney
item.description: Tom Moloney, Executive Strategy Director at Koto, argues that fintechs and established banks often end up chasing each other’s strengths as they grow. Fintechs have to prove they are safe and built to last, while banks have to feel faster and simpler. Their playbooks, he adds, now “often tell you the category, not the company,” which is why he wants finance brands to “stop treating creativity as the layer added at the end.” In our conversation, he draws on the global creative company’s work and examples from across the industry to explain what separates the strongest brands in the category, how a growing range of products can hold together, how brands can stay visible as more of their services happen in the background, and why easier access to investing leaves more firms fighting for the same customers.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: COPUS and Kontrapunkt design JUNO the bakery’s cookie brand and site
item.description: Since 2018, there has been a queue outside JUNO the bakery, which sits in a quiet corner of Copenhagen’s Østerbro district. Founded by Nina Schmiegelow and Emil Glaser, it is routinely named among the best bakeries in the world. With Danish Butter Cookies by JUNO the bakery, they are taking their first steps beyond the city. The cookies are handmade at JUNO’s facility in Nordvest, Copenhagen, and sold both in the bakery and through its first online shop. “For years, we wanted to make something that could travel, survive a suitcase and still taste like JUNO on the other side of the world,” Glaser tells us.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Estúdio 017’s identity for Garde refuses to tie itself to one logo
item.description: Garde is a non-profit foundation for contemporary art, fashion and cinema, based in Berlin and started by a collective of anonymous independent artists. Brazilian and Portuguese studio Estúdio 017 created its brand strategy, verbal identity, visual identity and editorial system ahead of its launch.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Local feel, one look: The Collected Works rebrands shuttle firm Circuit
item.description: Circuit is an on-demand electric shuttle service that works with cities to help people get around, often for free, mostly connecting them with local businesses, transit hubs and other nearby destinations. Founded by Alexander Esposito and James Mirras, it started in the Hamptons in 2011 and now runs in more than 50 US cities, where it has given more than 10 million rides – more than 16,000 a month in San Diego alone. New York City and New Orleans-based design studio The Collected Works was commissioned to rebrand Circuit, working across the identity, out-of-home, web, vehicle wraps, 3D, motion and copywriting.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: Seven years, then burnout: why Nika Belskaya has quit branding
item.description: Nika Belskaya has quit designing identities for clients to focus on her work as an artist through Vivid Cereal, her creative practice. Branding was meant to be a temporary financial safety net while she built her art, but seven years went by. The more clients she took on, the less time was left for anything else. In January 2026, she planned a slow shift away from client work, but financial fears had her saying yes to every commercial offer. By October, she was burned out. She announced her exit in her Substack piece ‘I’m Quitting Branding.’ She is also moving from Tbilisi to Berlin, where she sees more opportunities as an artist. In this interview, the designer behind Vivid Cereal talks about why she went public before landing anywhere safe and what she would say to designers who feel their vision fading through client work.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity

item.title: The New York Times turns 175 with an identity, events and a campaign
item.description: For its 175th anniversary, The New York Times created a custom 175 mark and identity system to use across editorial, opinion, advertising, events and marketing. The anniversary programme also included a celebration and exhibition at Spring Studios, plus a social campaign, film series, photojournalism tour of university campuses and an identity for The Times’s NYC Marathon team. Creative Director Jessi Brattengeier led the work alongside The Times’s in-house Culture and Comms Design team and a roster of select partners.
item.dc:creator: The Brand Identity
